criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Multiple ethical issues (public safety, integrity, business ethics) identified and linked to engineering design; both organisational context and stakeholder interests clearly demonstrated.

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Balanced for/against arguments with reasonable depth and a clear conclusion; however, decision-making recommendations for different stakeholders are limited to Rachel and her company.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Logically structured body building from economic arguments to safety, integrity and reputation, culminating in a supported conclusion. Compelling but some arguments (e.g. competitor shipping anyway) are left unresolved.

evidence.quote: Adhering to ethical frameworks such as the EACE is essential for the very existence of engineering as an industry

criteria.reasoning: Four relevant references including NHS IT-failure and Volkswagen case studies with quantitative evidence; depth is good but limited number of sources and no counter-evidence.

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: Fluent writing overall with all required sections, but no figures, tables or visual elements at all; minor typos and inconsistent reference formatting.

overall: A well-structured, fluent ethics report with balanced arguments, relevant case studies (NHS, Volkswagen) and a clear justified recommendation. Stakeholder analysis and evidence are strong, but the report lacks any visual elements and has minor formatting/typographical issues.

feedback.summary: A well-structured, fluent ethics report with balanced arguments, relevant case studies (NHS, Volkswagen) and a clear, justified recommendation. Your stakeholder analysis and evidence are strong, but the report lacks any visual elements, has minor typos, and reference formatting is inconsistent.
next_steps: Add visual elements such as a stakeholder table or decision-flow diagram to support your discussion and lift C5.
Resolve open arguments (e.g. whether competitors would ship defective products anyway) rather than leaving them hanging.
Broaden decision-making recommendations to more stakeholders (chip contractor, government health department) and add counter-evidence and more sources.
Fix reference formatting to consistent IEEE style, including URLs and access dates, and proofread headings/typos.

criteria.C1: Excellent: you identified several ethical issues (public safety, integrity, business ethics), linked them to engineering design, and clearly demonstrated both organisational context and stakeholder interests in your Introduction. Maintain this breadth in future work.
criteria.C2: Very good: your for/against arguments have appropriate depth and a clear conclusion, but decision-making recommendations cover mainly Rachel and her company. To reach Excellent, extend recommendations to other stakeholders such as the chip contractor and the health department.
criteria.C3: Very good: your body builds logically from economic to safety, integrity and reputation arguments and supports your conclusion well. To reach Excellent, resolve open arguments (e.g. the competitor-shipping point) so every thread strengthens the conclusion.
criteria.C4: Very good: the NHS and Volkswagen case studies with quantitative evidence substantiate your arguments well. To reach Excellent, use more sources and include counter-evidence to show a fully balanced, in-depth research base.
criteria.C5: Good: your writing is fluent with all required sections, but there are no figures, tables or visual elements, plus minor typos (e.g. 'DICUSSION') and inconsistent IEEE reference formatting. Adding visuals and polishing formatting would lift this substantially.
